tagline: Hazelnut groves, hillside vineyards and restored wetlands share the Tualatin Valley.
intro: The Vineyard and Valley Tour Route winds through the Tualatin Valley, passing orchards, hazelnut groves and vineyards against the Coast Range foothills. Travel Oregon describes a 57-mile drive taking two to five hours, with local produce and wine at the center of its appeal. Near Sherwood, the tour passes a restored floodplain at the Tualatin River National Wildlife Refuge, where trails, overlooks and a wildlife center welcome visitors.

Earlier transportation routes shaped the places this tour connects. Gaston grew from a railroad stop in 1872 into a commercial center. At Banks, a former railroad bed now serves as the Banks-Vernonia State Trail. Near Gaston, a different change reshaped the land: the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service began buying Wapato Lake bed property in 2008 to restore wetland.

Traveling from the Helvetia end toward Sherwood, the tour takes in Old Scotch Church and heads through Banks toward Gales Creek. The church’s eight-sided steeple belongs to its 1878 building. Continue toward Gaston through vineyard country, then through Laurelwood toward Sherwood as the route exchanges foothills for farm fields, orchards and wetlands. The Tualatin River refuge is the final landscape anchor near Sherwood.

moments.title: Old Scotch Church
moments.text: An eight-sided steeple rises from the 1878 Old Scotch Church, whose congregation began five years before its building. Its first members came primarily from the same part of Aberdeenshire, Scotland, and initially worshipped in a schoolhouse. For their permanent church, congregation members donated much of the material and labor. The Carpenter Gothic design combined buttresses and a steep roof with stained glass imported from Scotland. Joseph Meek’s remains were moved here from his homestead after that land was sold. The Tualatin Plains Presbyterian Church continues to worship in the building.
moments.notice: Look for the eight-sided steeple and the steep roof of the Carpenter Gothic church.

moments.title: Gaston
moments.text: Gaston’s namesake tried for sixteen years to turn Wapato Lake into farmland. Railroad executive Joseph Gaston moved here in 1880, after legal disputes ended his position with the railroad. The town had grown from an 1872 railroad stop. The Wapato Improvement District completed the drainage in the 1930s. The direction changed in 2008, when the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service began buying lakebed land to restore the wetland. People from the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community replanted wapato in the restored lake before the refuge’s March 2023 opening.

moments.title: Tualatin River National Wildlife Refuge
moments.text: Seasonal ponds are part of a deliberately restored landscape at the Tualatin River National Wildlife Refuge. Much of this land previously supported hog and dairy farms, corn and onions. In 1992, Tom Stibolt and Lisa Brenner donated the first 12 acres, which the Fish and Wildlife Service accepted to establish the refuge. Restoration began in 1997, when water-control systems and dikes were added so managers could flood portions of the land. Regular public access began in June 2006. The observation deck overlooks seasonal ponds; Travel Oregon also identifies trails and a wildlife center for visitors.
